topics.topic: Crash-safe durable publication protocol for database records and files
questions: What sequence and recovery rule guarantees that a committed record never names an absent or incomplete file across every crash point?
Does the guarantee cover only kernel-process termination or also host/power loss, and which file and directory synchronization steps are required before a store call succeeds?
What durability protocol must make the promised crash behavior hold across power loss, including consistency between a published file and the database record naming it?
Can a crash leave a committed record naming a missing file, and what exact ordering or recovery rule prevents or handles that state?
Does the guarantee cover process termination only, or also operating-system and power loss, and which durability operations are required before a store call succeeds?

quotes: record_change: [PATH_OR_ARTIFACT_POLICY] Durability order: every file a change names is published, fsynced and its directory fsynced before the change is committed, and the SQLite database runs with synchronous FULL, so after a power loss a committed record never names a missing or partial file; a file published by a change that then failed stays unnamed until the next start removes it (A18 rule 4).

put_value_bytes: [PATH_OR_ARTIFACT_POLICY] MUST store the bytes in the content-addressed area under their digest: when a file for that digest already exists it returns without writing; otherwise it writes a temporary file in the same area, flushes and fsyncs it, re-checks its digest and size, and renames it into place without overwriting, so a crash leaves either no file or the complete file and a completed file is never rewritten.
judgement.why: The later store notes define publication before commit, file and directory fsync, SQLite synchronous FULL, power-loss coverage and cleanup of unnamed residue.

topics.topic: Event that assigns the serial order of concurrent requests
questions: What event fixes concurrent requests' order, and at what point is a request admitted to the single processing queue?
What event establishes the total order of concurrent MCP requests?
At what event is a request assigned its serial position, and how are simultaneous arrivals ordered?

judgement.why: This is the same concurrent-request serialization question already judged from the unchanged later surface contract.

precedent.topic: Event that fixes concurrent request serialization order
quotes: serve_kernel: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] Requests are handled strictly one at a time, each to its end, run advancement included, before the next one is read (A18 rule 3).
precedent.why: The later surface contract establishes the total order by reading no next request until the current request has completed.

topics.topic: Exclusive-lock mechanism, ownership, failure classification, and crash release
questions: What constitutes the exclusive lock, how are permission or I/O failures classified, and does process death automatically release it without stale-lock recovery?
What lock mechanism and lifetime establish that a crashed process cannot permanently block a later start?
What constitutes ownership of the lock, when is it released, and may startup recover automatically after the previous process crashed?

quotes: open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on a lock file inside data_directory, opened without following links and held for the life of the process; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue and no file fixture record names, and create the database schema, the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.

open_store: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise RefusedError whose reason names the failed check: data_directory does not exist (it is never created here), lock held by another process, directory not private (naming the first offending path), or symbolic link found (naming its path); it removes and creates nothing when a check fails.

serve_kernel: [VALIDATION_ERROR] When run_start_sequence raises, MUST write the failing step and the exception's reason to standard error, without any token, credential value, configuration content or stack trace, open no entrance and return a non-zero exit code; there is no partial start and no retry. Ending the process releases the store lock; nothing the steps already committed is rolled back, and the next start runs the whole sequence again from those records. Binding the listener at mcp_listen_address is the last start step and fails the same way, the step named open_entrance, when the address cannot be parsed as a host and port or the socket cannot be bound; a listener lost while serving ends the process with a non-zero exit code, without retry.
judgement.why: The later notes specify a non-blocking process-held lock file, its lifetime, lock-held refusal and automatic release when the process ends.

topics.topic: Initial store artifacts and first-start data-directory creation
questions: Which store artifacts must already exist, and which may the kernel create on first start?
Which of these states initializes a new store, and which refuse startup?
May the kernel create the data directory, database, content areas, spool and schema on first start, or must they already exist?

judgement.why: This is the same first-start data-directory and store-object creation question already decided by the unchanged later store API.

precedent.topic: Creation requirements for missing data-directory and store objects
quotes: open_store: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise RefusedError whose reason names the failed check: data_directory does not exist (it is never created here), lock held by another process, directory not private (naming the first offending path), or symbolic link found (naming its path); it removes and creates nothing when a check fails.

The kernel never
creates the data directory itself: the owner creates it, private to the
kernel's user; inside it `open_store` creates the database schema, the
content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.
precedent.why: The later store API refuses a missing data directory but creates the database schema, content-addressed area, and spool area inside an existing valid directory.

topics.topic: Integrity checks and response to corrupt databases or missing or corrupt referenced content
questions: What integrity checks run at startup or first access, and does detected corruption stop the kernel, fail one request, or permit partial operation?
How does the kernel respond to database corruption or a committed record whose referenced bytes are missing or corrupt?
Does the kernel refuse to start, mark affected records unavailable, or repair/delete them when durable records and filesystem contents disagree?

quotes:
The data directory holds one SQLite database with every kernel record, a
   content-addressed area of value bytes and file fixtures named by digest, and
   the run spool, one subdirectory per run.

open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on a lock file inside data_directory, opened without following links and held for the life of the process; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue and no file fixture record names, and create the database schema, the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.

read_value_bytes: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise UnknownReferenceError when the identity names no record, and StoreInternalError when the bytes of an existing record are missing, unreadable, reached through a symbolic link, or differ from the record's digest or size.

show_port_refs: [VALIDATION_ERROR] A referenced StoredValue or SpooledFile that cannot be read, or bytes that cannot be read, is not skipped: the exception propagates, so the whole answer is internal_error and no partial answer is returned.
judgement.divergence: One implementation validates the database and all referenced content at startup and refuses the whole kernel on corruption; another starts normally and detects missing or corrupt bytes only when an affected record is read, allowing unrelated operations meanwhile. The owner and callers notice startup availability and whether unrelated requests continue to work.
judgement.why: The texts define access-time failure for bad referenced bytes but do not decide database-integrity validation or whether durable-store inconsistencies are detected eagerly, isolated lazily or repaired.

topics.topic: Ownership, permissions, and object types required for a private store

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged private-store ownership, permission and object-type topic previously judged preexisting.

precedent.topic: Ownership, file-type, permission, and link requirements for private store objects
quotes: The directory and everything in it are private to the kernel's user; the kernel refuses to start otherwise. Every file of the directory is opened without following symbolic links; a link found at start stops the start, and one found later makes that store call fail with nothing written.
precedent.why: The topic concerns the unchanged private-store and link-check passage, and the reopening change neither touched it nor made exact file types or hard-link counts newly consequential.

topics.topic: Record position ordering within and across store calls and updates
questions: What is the total store order, how are multiple records written by one store call ordered, and does updating a mutable record change its position?
What exactly is the store order, and is a record's position permanently assigned when it is first created?
In what order are positions assigned when one store call creates several records atomically?
What records receive positions, what is their order within one transaction, and does updating an entity's status preserve its original position or receive another position?

quotes: record_change: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] Every record written gets one store position from a single strictly increasing counter shared by all record types, assigned inside the transaction that writes it; store order is the order of these positions, every collection the module returns is in store order unless the function says otherwise, and Activation and FlowActivation records are identified by their store_position.

record_change: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] The records one change writes take their store positions in the order the FIELD_ASSIGNMENT note of its variant lists them, the elements of a list of records in list order (a value list's StoredValues before the record naming them, a RecordRunProgressChange's executions in (node_id, map_index) order); an update keeps the record's position, so positions never depend on record type or database insertion order.
judgement.why: The later store notes define a global counter, the within-change assignment order and permanent positions for updated records.

   bytes until the next start removes them (rule 4).

record_change: [BEHAVIOR] MUST apply the one StoreChange given in one SQLite transaction that either writes every record the variant lists or nothing; it writes no record the variant does not list and trusts the caller for every decision of the caller's rule, checking only its own invariants: attempt numbers, unique and existing identities, existing linked records, and no edit of an immutable record. Records of the kinds that are never edited — issued contract versions, implementations, trial cases, flow versions, values, verdicts, activations and trace records — are only ever written once; for any other entity a lifecycle change — a status, who decided, resolved, revoked, cancelled or released and when, concluded_at, ended_at, waiting points, outputs — updates those fields of the entity's one record in place, and the record keeps its store position, the position of its creation; no other field of a written record ever changes.

record_change: [VALIDATION_ERROR] For RecordAttemptOutcomeChange and RecoverInFlightChange MUST raise RefusedError, writing nothing, when the named attempt's attempt_number is no longer one more than the number of NodeExecutions of its element; the concluding NodeExecution then takes that attempt's number. Any other broken invariant (a linked record missing, an identity already present for an immutable record, a status change from a status the change does not start from) or a failed transaction raises StoreInternalError with nothing written.

answer_request: [ORCHESTRATION] MUST call the handler of the named operation, whose name is handle_ followed by the operation name, with the Actor and the validated request, encode its answer as the tool result — values as JSON text, file bytes as base64 — and turn any exception the handler raises into a refusal answer through translate_failure, except any failure translate_failure answers internal_error — StopRequiredError, StoreInternalError or any unexpected exception, whatever the handler — which it lets propagate to serve_kernel unchanged, since a store change may already be written and only the next start derives every run again.
judgement.divergence: After an SQLite commit returns an ambiguous error, one implementation reports internal_error and stops even if the transaction became durable; another verifies or recovers the transaction and reports success when it committed. The caller notices a different response, and the owner notices whether the durable change exists after restart.
judgement.why: The texts promise all-or-nothing records and describe ordinary failed transactions, but do not define how an uncertain commit is classified before the surface chooses success or internal_error.

topics.topic: Startup cleanup policy for unreferenced trial-fixture blobs
questions: Are unreferenced file-fixture blobs removed at startup under the same rule as unreferenced value bytes?
Are unreferenced published trial fixtures also removed at startup, or can a failed capture leave them indefinitely?

quotes: open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on a lock file inside data_directory, opened without following links and held for the life of the process; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue and no file fixture record names, and create the database schema, the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.
judgement.why: The later startup note explicitly removes content-addressed files whose digest is named by neither a StoredValue nor a file-fixture record.
